To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) pairwise aggregation holds if and only if all income expansion paths are parallel to the same line, (2) if pairwise aggregation holds, then there is a representative competitive consumer whose demand function is the mean demand, and (3) if the distribution of income can be changed, then there is always a distribution that makes the mean demand function competitive

the sufficient conditions for “representative” consumer demand to be the mean demand for the group are the same as those for pairwise aggregation, and that the necessary conditions are the same as the sufficient conditions except for the case of non-homothetic preferences.

the sufficient conditions are necessary and sufficient for pairwise aggregation, and that the necessary conditions imply that a representative consumer exists if the income expansion paths lie either in parallel planes or in the same plane, but do not otherwise imply that a representative exists.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the conditions under which the mean of a group of demand functions can be represented as the demand of a “representive” competitive consumer.
the conditions under which the demand of a group of individuals can be aggregated in the sense that the mean demand for a good satisfies the Slutsky conditions.
the question of when the demand of a representative consumer is equal to the mean demand of a group of individual consumers, when the income distribution is fixed.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the mean demand functions of a fixed group of consumers satisfy the Slutsky restrictions for every fixed income vector distribution if and only if either all the consumers have homogenous preferences or, alternatively and equivalently, for each price vector the consumers' income-expansion paths lie in a common plane.
the mean demand functions of the consumers in a group are pairwise aggregative if and only if the consumers are either homothetic or have income expansion paths that lie in the same fixed plane.

the mean demand functions satisfy the Slutsky restrictions if and only if the distribution of income can be changed in such a way that the mean demand function is the demand of some competitive representative consumer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the necessary and sufficient conditions are satisfied only if the consumers are homothetic, or if for each price system, the consumers' indifference curves all pass through a common point.
the necessary conditions for aggregation are more stringent than the sufficient conditions.

pairwise aggregation holds if and only if the consumers' preferences can be represented by a linear function of the income and the price vector, or by a homothetic function of the income expansion paths.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in contrast with the case of aggregation over consumers with different distributions of income, the existence of a representative competitive consumer is not guaranteed even in the absence of aggregation errors.
the necessary and sufficient conditions are not equivalent.
pairwise aggregation is a much stronger requirement than the existence of a representative consumer, which is only one of the sufficient conditions for pairwise aggregation.
